questions.question: Q-learning is proved to converge on an MDP. Why does that proof stop applying once a second learning agent shares the world?
options: The shared reward becomes unbounded once two agents can both collect it from the same terminal state
The other agent's changing policy is part of your transition and reward, so nothing is stationary
The joint state space becomes continuous once both agents' positions are tracked together
Two agents optimizing separate returns cannot share a single discount factor
questions.explanation: The convergence argument leans on fixed P and R. When the other agent learns, the effective dynamics move underneath you every update, so there is no fixed point for the Bellman operator to contract to.

questions.question: In centralized training with decentralized execution, what exactly is centralized?
options: Every agent shares one policy network during training, but each keeps a private critic fitted to its own reward stream
The critic sees the global state and the joint action during training, while each policy conditions only on its own observation at execution time
Both the policy and the critic condition on the full global state and the joint action at training time and at execution time; only the reward stays per-agent
The replay buffer is shared, and every stored transition is relabelled with the opponents' current policies before it is reused
questions.explanation: The critic is a training-time object you can throw away, so it is allowed to cheat with global information. The actor is what gets deployed, so it must live on local observations alone.

questions.question: On the 5×5 cooperative GridWorld the joint-Q table stores 16 entries per state instead of two tables of 4. What is the trade you just made?
options: A correct global view, paid for with an action space exponential in the agent count
You gained sample efficiency, since 16 finer-grained entries generalize better than 4 coarse ones
You removed the need for ε-greedy exploration, because the joint argmax already covers every pair
You made execution decentralized, since each agent can read the shared table and pick its own component
questions.explanation: |A|ⁿ entries per state is the whole problem with the joint approach: correct here with 2 agents and 4 actions, hopeless at n = 10. It is also the least decentralized option, since an agent needs the other's choice to pick the argmax.

questions.question: COMA's counterfactual baseline computes an advantage how?
options: My return on the episode minus the average return the other agents collected over that same episode
The joint Q minus the sum of the per-agent Qs, which is the monotonic value decomposition QMIX uses to keep the argmax decentralized
My Q minus the expectation of Q over my own action choices, holding the other agents' actions fixed
The TD residual computed on each agent's local observation only
questions.explanation: Marginalizing over my action while freezing everyone else's isolates what my choice contributed to the shared reward. That is the credit-assignment question a single shared reward otherwise leaves unanswerable.

questions.question: You change the task so the goal only counts when both agents step onto it on the same turn. Independent Q-learning, which solved the original task, now stalls. Why?
options: The reward is now sparse, so the discount factor must be lowered to keep the bootstrap targets from washing out over the longer episodes the coordination task produces
The state space grew, so the two Q-tables no longer fit the reachable joint positions
The task became tightly coupled: my best action depends on the other's simultaneous choice, which independent learners cannot represent
ε-greedy exploration stops being valid once the goal requires two synchronized arrivals
questions.explanation: Independent learners each treat the other as noise, so a payoff that exists only for one specific action pair looks like a rare accident. Coupling — not sparsity or table size — is the thing that broke.

questions.question: When is pure self-play not enough, so you need a league of past policies and exploiters?
options: Whenever there are more than two agents, since self-play only ever pits one policy against a single copy of itself
When the game admits rock-paper-scissors strategy cycles, so beating the current best does not mean being globally strong
When the reward is shared rather than zero-sum, because a cooperative task gives self-play no adversarial pressure to keep improving
When the policy is too large to snapshot cheaply, so a league of past checkpoints costs more memory than the run can afford
questions.explanation: Self-play only ever asks 'can I beat my recent self', which a dominance cycle satisfies forever without progress. A diverse opponent pool plus exploiters keeps the training signal from collapsing onto one branch of the cycle.
